content: Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is a chronic condition characterized by symptoms resulting from damage to the esophageal mucosa caused by the abnormal reflux of acidic stomach contents into the esophagus. This condition often arises due to transient or permanent alterations in the barrier between the esophagus and the stomach. These changes may include incompetence of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES), transient relaxation of the LES, impaired clearance of gastric reflux from the esophagus, or the presence of a hiatal hernia. Chronic GERD is associated with an increased risk of Barrett's esophagus, a premalignant condition of the esophageal mucosa, which in turn is linked to a higher likelihood of developing esophageal adenocarcinoma. Historically, GERD is believed to have been first described and treated by the ancient Egyptians, as evidenced by papyrus records discovered by Edwin Smith in Thebes. The term esophagus was coined by the ancient Greeks. In 1925, Friedenwald and Feldman described the symptoms of GERD, and in 1926, Robbins and Jankelson utilized radiological techniques to observe the condition. GERD can be classified based on the endoscopic appearance of the esophageal mucosa and the clinical presentation of the disease. The pathophysiology of GERD involves several mechanisms that contribute to the retrograde movement of acidic stomach contents into the esophagus. These mechanisms include transient relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter, hypotensive LES, hiatal hernia, and prolonged esophageal acid clearance. Common causes of GERD include obesity, autonomic neuropathy, systemic sclerosis, esophageal achalasia, and hiatal hernia. Other causes include hypochlorhydria, hypercalcemia, and Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. GERD must be differentiated from other conditions such as gastritis, peptic ulcer disease, Crohn's disease, gastric adenocarcinoma, and gastrinoma. The prevalence of GERD in the United States and Europe ranges from 10,000 to 20,000 cases per 100,000 people. The incidence of GERD increases with age, particularly in individuals over 40 years old. Common risk factors for GERD include smoking, obesity, pregnancy, alcohol binge drinking, and the use of medications such as anticholinergic drugs. Additional risk factors include the consumption of certain foods, such as spicy foods, and poor eating habits, such as consuming large meals. There is insufficient evidence to recommend routine screening for GERD. If left untreated, approximately 20% of patients with GERD may develop esophageal strictures due to excessive acid exposure in the lower esophagus. Complications of GERD include Barrett's esophagus, erosive esophagitis, esophageal ulcers, and esophageal adenocarcinoma. The prognosis of GERD is favorable with appropriate treatment. The diagnosis of GERD is based on a combination of history, symptoms, and diagnostic studies. Common symptoms include heartburn, regurgitation, and dysphagia. A history of nausea, vomiting, and regurgitation is suggestive of GERD. Other symptoms may include chest pain, cough, and odynophagia. On physical examination, patients with GERD may appear unwell due to pain. Findings may include hoarseness of voice, laryngitis, otitis media, and lung wheezes. Laboratory findings consistent with GERD include the detection of acidic reflux in the esophagus through ambulatory reflux monitoring. Electrocardiogram (EKG) findings are not associated with GERD, but EKG may be performed to rule out cardiac causes of chest pain in cases of atypical GERD. X-ray imaging may reveal associated problems such as free acid reflux, esophagitis with scarring, strictures, and Barrett's esophagus. There are no specific findings on CT scans, MRI scans, or ultrasound associated with GERD. However, endoscopy may be used to screen for complications of chronic GERD, such as Barrett's esophagus. The primary treatment for GERD involves lifestyle modifications, including weight loss, elevating the head of the bed, and avoiding eating before sleep. Pharmacologic therapy is recommended for patients with persistent GERD despite lifestyle changes. Medications used in the treatment of GERD include antacids, histamine receptor antagonists, proton pump inhibitors, and prokinetic agents. Surgery is not the first-line treatment for GERD and is typically reserved for patients with chronic GERD, high volumes of acid reflux, non-compliance with medical therapy, large hiatal hernias, or upper respiratory manifestations such as hoarseness and laryngitis. The Nissen fundoplication is the surgical procedure of choice for GERD. Primary prevention of GERD includes avoiding foods that exacerbate symptoms, smoking cessation, weight loss, eating smaller and more frequent meals, and elevating the head of the bed while sleeping.
